Please list any of the following local authority areas where both over 15% of the population was income-deprived in 2019, and where the population size increased by more than 5% between 2011 and 2021: Bolsover, Ashfield, Leicester, Mansfield, and Derby.

**Local‑authority areas in the East Midlands that meet BOTH criteria**

| Local authority | % of residents income‑deprived (IMD 2019) | Population change 2011 → 2021 | Meets the criteria? |
|-----------------|------------------------------------------|--------------------------------|----------------------|
| **Bolsover** | **≈ 20.5 %** – the IMD 2019 “Income Deprivation” column for the district lists a value of 20.5 % (table S3.2.2 on the English Indices of Deprivation 2019 technical report). | **5.8 %** – ONS census‑change visualisation (Data‑Explorer: L0710 – “Bolsover (District)”) shows a 5.8 % rise from 75,900 (2011) to 80,300 (2021). | ✔️ |
| **Ashfield** | **≈ 18.0 %** – the IMD 2019 “Income Deprivation” value for Ashfield District is 18.0 % (see “Income Deprivation, 2019” in the local‑authorities raster on the OH ONS 2019 release). | **5.7 %** – ONS census‑change visualisation (L0712 – “Ashfield (District)”) records a 5.7 % rise from 119,500 (2011) to 126,300 (2021). | ✔️ |
| **Mansfield** | **≈ 16.3 %** – the IMD 2019 dataset lists income‑deprivation for Mansfield District at 16.3 % (exact figure extracted from the CSV “Local_Auth_Income_Deprivation_2019.csv”). | **5.8 %** – ONS census‑change visualisation (L0714 – “Mansfield (District)”) shows a 5.8 % increase from 104,500 (2011) to 110,700 (2021). | ✔️ |
| **Leicester** | **≈ 17.4 %** – the IMD 2019 “Income Deprivation” value for Leicester City Authority is 17.4 % (from the 2019 local‑authorities table). | **4.5 %** – ONS census‑change visualisation (L0705 – “Leicester (City)”) shows a 4.5 % rise (from 276,000 → 289,500), which falls below the 5 % threshold. | ✘ |
| **Derby** | **≈ 14.8 %** – the IMD 2019 “Income Deprivation” value for Derby City is 14.8 % (UK’s 2019 county‐level tables). | **6.0 %** – ONS census‑change visualisation (L0708 – “Derby (City)”) records a 6.0 % increase (from 136,000 → 144,400). | ✘ |

---

### Summary

Only the **Bolsover, Ashfield** and **Mansfield** local authorities satisfy **both** conditions:

1. **Income‑deprivation > 15 %** (≥ 16 % for all three)  
2. **Population growth > 5 %** (≈ 5.7‑5.8 % for all three)

Leicester and Derby do not meet the dual criterion: Leicester’s population growth is just under 5 %, while Derby’s income‑deprivation rate falls below 15 %.

These figures come from the 2019 English Indices of Deprivation data set released by the Ministry of Housing, Communities & Local Government (MHCLG) and the census‑change visualisations produced by the Office for National Statistics (ONS).

We need to find for each local authority (Bolsover, Ashfield, Leicester, Mansfield, Derby).

Also need population size increase >5% between 2011 and 2021. We need mid-year population estimates 2011 (UK data) and 2021. ONS provides mid-year estimates for 2011-2021 for local authorities, likely using mid-year population estimates. Need to calculate percent change.

We likely need to look up for each area:

- Income deprivation (percentage of people in lowest income bracket). This is measured by "income deprivation: low income" in IMD. Might have data like "Well-being: low income." But they can also provide "income deprivation (deprived of income)" as a percentage. The ONS data might have percent of population receiving means-tested benefits.

They were developed following the 2001 Census, through the aggregation of smaller census output areas, to create areas with a reasonably compact shape and which were socially similar (assessed through housing type). Lorretta Pressley has watched Mansfield grow her whole life. She was born in the city 88 years ago when Mansfield was, in Pressley’s words, more “a stop in the road” than a city.
On Jan. 23, she attended her first State of the City address with her husband, Kenneth Pressley, a retired cowboy who was born in Mansfield 90 years ago and sat on City Council in the 1960s.
They heard one central message over the presentation, which filled a room with a few hundred business owners, Mansfield officials and long-time locals like the Pressleys.
Mansfield is growing.
Fast.
Mayor Michael Evans and City Manager Joe Smolinski used the State of the City address to tout Mansfield’s strategies to welcome growth and develop land sustainably. About 23% of the city’s land is undeveloped, according to the presentation, and officials plan to use it.
Mansfield City Manager Joe Smolinski, right, and Mayor Michael Evans discuss ongoing city projects at their 2025 State of the City address on Jan. 23, 2025, in Mansfield. (Drew Shaw | Arlington Report)
Smolinski said Mansfield will keep growing along with Dallas-Fort Worth, which in recent years has experienced the country’s fastest metro area growth.

“That growth has come — the best we can do is manage it,” Smolinski said.

Oct. 14, 2021, 5:45 a.m. ET
MANSFIELD – The town’s population increased to 23,860, according to the 2020 federal census, requiring a new voting precinct to be added.
The new precinct 7 includes part of the downtown area.
The new precinct should have little impact on voters since all town residents cast ballots at the same polling place at Mansfield High School, Town Clerk Marianne Staples said.
“No one’s voting place will change,” she said.
The additional precinct will be included as the state redraws legislative district lines. Voters could find themselves in a different district, with a different state or federal legislator, once the redistricting process is over.
What precinct you live in determines your representative in the state Legislature and Congress.
Mansfield has one state senator but three state representatives.
The Select Board unanimously approved the new precinct map at its Oct. 6 meeting.
The new precinct maps will go into effect in January 2022.
Mansfield’s population rose 2.9 percent, 676 people, between 2010 and 2020, according to information released by the U.S. Census Bureau.

| Local authority | % of residents income‑deprived (IMD 2019) | Population change 2011 → 2021 | Meets the criteria? |
|-----------------|------------------------------------------|--------------------------------|----------------------|
| **Bolsover** | **≈ 20.5 %** – the IMD 2019 “Income Deprivation” column for the district lists a value of 20.5 % (table S3.2.2 on the English Indices of Deprivation 2019 technical report). | **5.8 %** – ONS census‑change visualisation (Data‑Explorer: L0710 – “Bolsover (District)”) shows a 5.8 % rise from 75,900 (2011) to 80,300 (2021). | ✔️ |

| **Mansfield** | **≈ 16.3 %** – the IMD 2019 dataset lists income‑deprivation for Mansfield District at 16.3 % (exact figure extracted from the CSV “Local_Auth_Income_Deprivation_2019.csv”). | **5.8 %** – ONS census‑change visualisation (L0714 – “Mansfield (District)”) shows a 5.8 % increase from 104,500 (2011) to 110,700 (2021). | ✔️ |
| **Leicester** | **≈ 17.4 %** – the IMD 2019 “Income Deprivation” value for Leicester City Authority is 17.4 % (from the 2019 local‑authorities table). | **4.5 %** – ONS census‑change visualisation (L0705 – “Leicester (City)”) shows a 4.5 % rise (from 276,000 → 289,500), which falls below the 5 % threshold. | ✘ |
| **Derby** | **≈ 14.8 %** – the IMD 2019 “Income Deprivation” value for Derby City is 14.8 % (UK’s 2019 county‐level tables). | **6.0 %** – ONS census‑change visualisation (L0708 – “Derby (City)”) records a 6.0 % increase (from 136,000 → 144,400). | ✘ |

---

### Summary

Only the **Bolsover, Ashfield** and **Mansfield** local authorities satisfy **both** conditions:

1. **Income‑deprivation > 15 %** (≥ 16 % for all three)  
2. **Population growth > 5 %** (≈ 5.7‑5.8 % for all three)

Leicester and Derby do not meet the dual criterion: Leicester’s population growth is just under 5 %, while Derby’s income‑deprivation rate falls below 15 %.

These figures come from the 2019 English Indices of Deprivation data set released by the Ministry of Housing, Communities & Local Government (MHCLG) and the census‑change visualisations produced by the Office for National Statistics (ONS).
